episodes.title: Why the Tech Right Lost Big This Week
episodes.about: Roose and Newton sit down with New York Times reporters Erin Griffith and Theodore Schleifer and columnist Ezra Klein to make sense of the midterm results for the tech industry: the role anti-AI and anti-data-center sentiment played, the backlash against billionaires, and whether Silicon Valley is having a vibe shift away from the Tech Right. Schleifer also ranks the midterm tech megadonors from first to worst on what they actually got for their money.
episodes.why: Out today, and the one episode that ties the week's politics directly to AI: anti-AI and anti-data-center sentiment as an actual election force, plus a donor-by-donor accounting of what Silicon Valley's midterm money bought.

episodes.title: Anthropic Study: Analysts Followed a Biased AI’s Lead 86% of the Time
episodes.about: An Anthropic experiment finds analysts followed the lean of biased AI agents 86% of the time. The crew also covers GPT 6.2 Astra showing up in Codex usage breakdowns, new Anthropic research that uses cryptographic proofs to verify which model produced an output, and a Stanford test of 20 recent models that found half of 50 widely cited AI flaws gone but more sycophancy than before. Ethan Mollick's question about which skills humans should refuse to automate gets a full discussion.
episodes.why: A number worth remembering: when Anthropic leaned its agents, analysts followed the bias 86% of the time. The Stanford re-test in the same episode - half of 50 cited flaws fixed, sycophancy worse - is the other half of the picture.

episodes.title: The promise and risks of AI for mental health support
episodes.about: A growing number of lawsuits accuse AI companies of harming users - alleging chatbots have encouraged self-harm, reinforced delusions, or failed to recognize signs of distress. At the same time, a growing number of users, particularly younger ones, say they are turning to AI for emotional support. Dr. John Torous, who studies how technology interacts with mental health, explains why the same tool can help some people and put others at risk.
episodes.why: Twelve minutes on the sharpest version of the chatbot question, with a researcher who studies it: lawsuits on one side, younger users turning to chatbots for support on the other, and what the evidence actually shows.

episodes.title: Napster Is an AI Company Now. Seriously.
episodes.about: Corey talks with Napster CEO John Acunto about the company's pivot from music into AI agents and what Napster calls 'streaming intelligence.' Acunto lays out a four-part customer-data framework - capture, learn, act, own - and argues companies should use conversational agents to learn directly from customers while keeping control of the resulting data and models. The conversation covers photorealistic video agents, edge compute, and Napster's bet that the next AI interface will feel more like talking to a person than typing into a box.
episodes.why: Napster, the file-sharing name from 1999, now sells AI agents. Its CEO lays out the pivot in concrete terms - a four-part data framework and video agents you talk to - instead of a rebrand announcement.

episodes.title: Why Companies Are Paying You to Quit
episodes.about: Microsoft has announced buyouts for 60,000 employees, and WSJ reporter Chip Cutter says the programs are becoming a trend across corporate America. Companies under pressure to increase AI spending and cut costs see buyouts as a way to shrink headcount without the disruption and backlash that come with mass layoffs. Imani Moise hosts.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — The Journal. is the Wall Street Journal's daily news show, new here: Microsoft is paying 60,000 people to quit, and buyouts are spreading as companies free up money for AI spending without calling it layoffs.
